About the question text

Each NCERT question is shown in full above its solution, with its textbook location. The solutions are our own. This chapter has no intext questions. Exercises 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 have 44 numbered questions and 93 parts, and every part is solved separately below. Exercise 5.4 is marked by NCERT as optional — "not from the examination point of view" — and its five questions are solved at the end in a separate Challenge — not for the exam section.

How every solution is laid out: Given / Asked → Concept used (and why it applies here) → Steps, one per line, with the reason in words → Check → ✅ Final answer → Common trap.

Exercise 5.1

Exercise 5.1, Q1 (i)Taxi fare2 marks

In which of the following situations, does the list of numbers involved make an arithmetic progression, and why?
(i) The taxi fare after each km when the fare is ₹ 15 for the first km and ₹ 8 for each additional km.

Given: ₹ 15 for the first km, ₹ 8 for each further km. Asked: whether the fares after 1, 2, 3, … km form an AP, and why.

Concept used: a list is an AP if every term after the first is the term before it plus the same number (Topic 2). Why it applies: we can write the fares and check the differences.

  1. 1

    Fare after 1 km: ₹ 15. After 2 km: 15+8=2315 + 8 = 2315+8=23. After 3 km: 23+8=3123 + 8 = 3123+8=31. After 4 km: 31+8=3931 + 8 = 3931+8=39.

  2. 2

    The list is 15,23,31,39,…15, 23, 31, 39, \ldots15,23,31,39,…; the differences are 8,8,88, 8, 88,8,8.

  3. 3

    Each fare is the previous fare plus the same ₹ 8, so it is an AP with a=15a = 15a=15, d=8d = 8d=8.

  4. Check: the fare after n km is 15+8(n−1)15 + 8(n - 1)15+8(n−1): for n=4n = 4n=4 this is 15+24=3915 + 24 = 3915+24=39 ✔.

  5. Answer Yes. The fares (in ₹) 15,23,31,…15, 23, 31, \ldots15,23,31,… form an AP, because each one is obtained by adding ₹ 8 to the one before (d=8d = 8d=8).

    Common trap: Writing the list as 15,8,8,8,…15, 8, 8, 8, \ldots15,8,8,8,… (the charge for each km on its own). The question asks for the fare after each km — the running fare.
Exercise 5.1, Q1 (ii)Air in a cylinder2 marks

In which of the following situations, does the list of numbers involved make an arithmetic progression, and why?
(ii) The amount of air present in a cylinder when a vacuum pump removes 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ of the air remaining in the cylinder at a time.

Given: each stroke removes 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ of the air that is left. Asked: whether the amounts form an AP.

Concept used: check whether the same number is added each time (Topic 2). Why it applies: we can write the amounts in terms of the starting amount V.

  1. 1

    Let the cylinder start with V units of air.

  2. 2

    After one stroke, 34\dfrac{3}{4}43​ of it is left: 3V4\dfrac{3V}{4}43V​. After two strokes: 34×3V4=9V16\dfrac{3}{4} \times \dfrac{3V}{4} = \dfrac{9V}{16}43​×43V​=169V​.

  3. 3

    The list is V,3V4,9V16,…V, \dfrac{3V}{4}, \dfrac{9V}{16}, \ldotsV,43V​,169V​,…

  4. 4

    Differences: 3V4−V=−V4\dfrac{3V}{4} - V = -\dfrac{V}{4}43V​−V=−4V​ and 9V16−3V4=−3V16\dfrac{9V}{16} - \dfrac{3V}{4} = -\dfrac{3V}{16}169V​−43V​=−163V​. They are not equal.

  5. Check: each amount is 34\dfrac{3}{4}43​ times the one before — a multiplying pattern, not an adding one ✔.

  6. Answer No. The amounts V,3V4,(34)2V,…V, \dfrac{3V}{4}, \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 V, \ldotsV,43V​,(43​)2V,… do not have a common difference: each stroke removes less air than the one before.

    Common trap: Thinking "the same fraction is removed each time, so it is an AP". The same fraction of a smaller amount is a smaller amount.
Exercise 5.1, Q1 (iii)Digging a well2 marks

In which of the following situations, does the list of numbers involved make an arithmetic progression, and why?
(iii) The cost of digging a well after every metre of digging, when it costs ₹ 150 for the first metre and rises by ₹ 50 for each subsequent metre.

Given: ₹ 150 for the first metre; each later metre costs ₹ 50 more than the one before. Asked: whether the costs form an AP.

Concept used: a constant difference makes an AP (Topic 2). Why it applies: we can list the cost metre by metre.

  1. 1

    The cost of the 1st metre is ₹ 150, of the 2nd metre ₹ 200, of the 3rd ₹ 250, and so on.

  2. 2

    The list is 150,200,250,300,…150, 200, 250, 300, \ldots150,200,250,300,…; each difference is 50.

  3. 3

    So it is an AP with a=150a = 150a=150, d=50d = 50d=50.

  4. Check: the cost of the nth metre is 150+50(n−1)150 + 50(n - 1)150+50(n−1); the 4th metre costs 150+150=300150 + 150 = 300150+150=300 ✔.

  5. Answer Yes. The costs (in ₹) 150,200,250,…150, 200, 250, \ldots150,200,250,… form an AP with common difference 50.

    Common trap: Reading "the cost of digging … after every metre" as the total paid so far: 150, 350, 600, … These totals are not an AP (differences 200, 250, …). NCERT's answer takes each term as the cost of digging that metre, as above.
Exercise 5.1, Q1 (iv)Compound interest2 marks

In which of the following situations, does the list of numbers involved make an arithmetic progression, and why?
(iv) The amount of money in the account every year, when ₹ 10000 is deposited at compound interest at 8 % per annum.

Given: ₹ 10000 at 8% per annum, compounded yearly. Asked: whether the yearly amounts form an AP.

Concept used: check the differences (Topic 2). Why it applies: compound interest multiplies the amount by 1+8100=1.081 + \dfrac{8}{100} = 1.081+1008​=1.08 each year.

  1. 1

    After 1 year: 10000×1.08=1080010000 \times 1.08 = 1080010000×1.08=10800.

  2. 2

    After 2 years: 10800×1.08=1166410800 \times 1.08 = 1166410800×1.08=11664.

  3. 3

    After 3 years: 11664×1.08=12597.1211664 \times 1.08 = 12597.1211664×1.08=12597.12.

  4. 4

    Differences: 11664−10800=86411664 - 10800 = 86411664−10800=864 and 12597.12−11664=933.1212597.12 - 11664 = 933.1212597.12−11664=933.12. They are not equal.

  5. Check: with simple interest the amount would grow by the same ₹ 800 every year — an AP. Compound interest also earns interest on the interest, so the yearly increase keeps growing ✔.

  6. Answer No. The amounts 10000(1+8100)10000\left(1 + \dfrac{8}{100}\right)10000(1+1008​), 10000(1+8100)210000\left(1 + \dfrac{8}{100}\right)^210000(1+1008​)2, 10000(1+8100)3,…10000\left(1 + \dfrac{8}{100}\right)^3, \ldots10000(1+1008​)3,… do not have a common difference.

    Common trap: Treating compound interest like simple interest and adding ₹ 800 every year.
Exercise 5.1, Q2 (i)1 mark

Write first four terms of the AP, when the first term a and the common difference d are given as follows:
(i) a=10a = 10a=10, d=10d = 10d=10

Given: a=10a = 10a=10, d=10d = 10d=10. Asked: the first four terms.

Concept used: each term = the term before it + d (Topic 2). Why it applies: we know where to start and what to add.

  1. 1

    a1=10a_1 = 10a1​=10, a2=10+10=20a_2 = 10 + 10 = 20a2​=10+10=20, a3=20+10=30a_3 = 20 + 10 = 30a3​=20+10=30, a4=30+10=40a_4 = 30 + 10 = 40a4​=30+10=40.

  2. Check: a4=a+3d=10+30=40a_4 = a + 3d = 10 + 30 = 40a4​=a+3d=10+30=40 ✔.

  3. Answer 10,20,30,4010, 20, 30, 4010,20,30,40

    Common trap: Starting with a+da + da+d as the first term. The first term is a itself.
Exercise 5.1, Q2 (ii)1 mark

Write first four terms of the AP, when the first term a and the common difference d are given as follows:
(ii) a=−2a = -2a=−2, d=0d = 0d=0

Given: a=−2a = -2a=−2, d=0d = 0d=0. Asked: the first four terms.

Concept used: add d each time (Topic 2). Why it applies: adding 0 leaves every term unchanged.

  1. 1

    a1=−2a_1 = -2a1​=−2, and adding 0 each time gives −2,−2,−2-2, -2, -2−2,−2,−2.

  2. Check: a4=−2+3×0=−2a_4 = -2 + 3 \times 0 = -2a4​=−2+3×0=−2 ✔.

  3. Answer −2,−2,−2,−2-2, -2, -2, -2−2,−2,−2,−2

    Common trap: Thinking a list with d=0d = 0d=0 "is not an AP". It is — the common difference is 0.
Exercise 5.1, Q2 (iii)1 mark

Write first four terms of the AP, when the first term a and the common difference d are given as follows:
(iii) a=4a = 4a=4, d=−3d = -3d=−3

Given: a=4a = 4a=4, d=−3d = -3d=−3. Asked: the first four terms.

Concept used: add d each time (Topic 2). Why it applies: adding −3-3−3 means subtracting 3.

  1. 1

    444; 4+(−3)=14 + (-3) = 14+(−3)=1; 1+(−3)=−21 + (-3) = -21+(−3)=−2; −2+(−3)=−5-2 + (-3) = -5−2+(−3)=−5.

  2. Check: a4=4+3×(−3)=−5a_4 = 4 + 3 \times (-3) = -5a4​=4+3×(−3)=−5 ✔.

  3. Answer 4,1,−2,−54, 1, -2, -54,1,−2,−5

    Common trap: Getting the fourth term as −1-1−1 by subtracting 3 from +2+2+2 instead of from −2-2−2. Below zero, subtracting 3 makes the number more negative.
Exercise 5.1, Q2 (iv)1 mark

Write first four terms of the AP, when the first term a and the common difference d are given as follows:
(iv) a=−1a = -1a=−1, d=12d = \dfrac{1}{2}d=21​

Given: a=−1a = -1a=−1, d=12d = \dfrac{1}{2}d=21​. Asked: the first four terms.

Concept used: add d each time (Topic 2). Why it applies: d is a fraction, so add halves.

  1. 1

    −1-1−1; −1+12=−12-1 + \dfrac{1}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}−1+21​=−21​; −12+12=0-\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 0−21​+21​=0; 0+12=120 + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}0+21​=21​.

  2. Check: a4=−1+3×12=12a_4 = -1 + 3 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}a4​=−1+3×21​=21​ ✔.

  3. Answer −1,−12,0,12-1, -\dfrac{1}{2}, 0, \dfrac{1}{2}−1,−21​,0,21​

    Common trap: Writing −1+12=−32-1 + \dfrac{1}{2} = -\dfrac{3}{2}−1+21​=−23​. Adding a positive number moves the value up, towards 0.
Exercise 5.1, Q2 (v)1 mark

Write first four terms of the AP, when the first term a and the common difference d are given as follows:
(v) a=−1.25a = -1.25a=−1.25, d=−0.25d = -0.25d=−0.25

Given: a=−1.25a = -1.25a=−1.25, d=−0.25d = -0.25d=−0.25. Asked: the first four terms.

Concept used: add d each time (Topic 2). Why it applies: adding −0.25-0.25−0.25 moves each term 0.25 further below zero.

  1. 1

    −1.25-1.25−1.25; −1.25+(−0.25)=−1.50-1.25 + (-0.25) = -1.50−1.25+(−0.25)=−1.50; −1.50+(−0.25)=−1.75-1.50 + (-0.25) = -1.75−1.50+(−0.25)=−1.75; −1.75+(−0.25)=−2.00-1.75 + (-0.25) = -2.00−1.75+(−0.25)=−2.00.

  2. Check: a4=−1.25+3×(−0.25)=−1.25−0.75=−2a_4 = -1.25 + 3 \times (-0.25) = -1.25 - 0.75 = -2a4​=−1.25+3×(−0.25)=−1.25−0.75=−2 ✔.

  3. Answer −1.25,−1.50,−1.75,−2.00-1.25, -1.50, -1.75, -2.00−1.25,−1.50,−1.75,−2.00

    Common trap: Writing −1.25+(−0.25)=−1.00-1.25 + (-0.25) = -1.00−1.25+(−0.25)=−1.00. Two negatives added give a more negative number.
Exercise 5.1, Q3 (i)1 mark

For the following APs, write the first term and the common difference:
(i) 3,1,−1,−3,…3, 1, -1, -3, \ldots3,1,−1,−3,…

Given: an AP. Asked: a and d.

Concept used: a is the first term; d=a2−a1d = a_2 - a_1d=a2​−a1​ (Topic 2). Why it applies: the list is stated to be an AP, so one difference is enough.

  1. 1

    a=3a = 3a=3.

  2. 2

    d=a2−a1=1−3=−2d = a_2 - a_1 = 1 - 3 = -2d=a2​−a1​=1−3=−2.

  3. Check: −1−1=−2-1 - 1 = -2−1−1=−2 and −3−(−1)=−2-3 - (-1) = -2−3−(−1)=−2 ✔.

  4. Answer a=3a = 3a=3, d=−2d = -2d=−2

    Common trap: d=3−1=2d = 3 - 1 = 2d=3−1=2 — subtracting the wrong way round. The list goes down, so d is negative.
Exercise 5.1, Q3 (ii)1 mark

For the following APs, write the first term and the common difference:
(ii) −5,−1,3,7,…-5, -1, 3, 7, \ldots−5,−1,3,7,…

Given: an AP. Asked: a and d.

Concept used: d=a2−a1d = a_2 - a_1d=a2​−a1​ (Topic 2). Why it applies: the list is an AP.

  1. 1

    a=−5a = -5a=−5.

  2. 2

    d=−1−(−5)=−1+5=4d = -1 - (-5) = -1 + 5 = 4d=−1−(−5)=−1+5=4.

  3. Check: 3−(−1)=43 - (-1) = 43−(−1)=4 and 7−3=47 - 3 = 47−3=4 ✔.

  4. Answer a=−5a = -5a=−5, d=4d = 4d=4

    Common trap: −1−(−5)-1 - (-5)−1−(−5) written as −6-6−6. Subtracting a negative means adding.
Exercise 5.1, Q3 (iii)1 mark

For the following APs, write the first term and the common difference:
(iii) 13,53,93,133,…\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{5}{3}, \dfrac{9}{3}, \dfrac{13}{3}, \ldots31​,35​,39​,313​,…

Given: an AP of fractions with the same denominator. Asked: a and d.

Concept used: d=a2−a1d = a_2 - a_1d=a2​−a1​ (Topic 2). Why it applies: same denominators make subtraction easy.

  1. 1

    a=13a = \dfrac{1}{3}a=31​.

  2. 2

    d=53−13=43d = \dfrac{5}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}d=35​−31​=34​.

  3. Check: 93−53=43\dfrac{9}{3} - \dfrac{5}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}39​−35​=34​ and 133−93=43\dfrac{13}{3} - \dfrac{9}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}313​−39​=34​ ✔.

  4. Answer a=13a = \dfrac{1}{3}a=31​, d=43d = \dfrac{4}{3}d=34​

    Common trap: Simplifying 93\dfrac{9}{3}39​ to 3 and then subtracting 3−533 - \dfrac{5}{3}3−35​ wrongly. Keep the common denominator.
Exercise 5.1, Q3 (iv)1 mark

For the following APs, write the first term and the common difference:
(iv) 0.6,1.7,2.8,3.9,…0.6, 1.7, 2.8, 3.9, \ldots0.6,1.7,2.8,3.9,…

Given: an AP of decimals. Asked: a and d.

Concept used: d=a2−a1d = a_2 - a_1d=a2​−a1​ (Topic 2). Why it applies: the list is an AP.

  1. 1

    a=0.6a = 0.6a=0.6.

  2. 2

    d=1.7−0.6=1.1d = 1.7 - 0.6 = 1.1d=1.7−0.6=1.1.

  3. Check: 2.8−1.7=1.12.8 - 1.7 = 1.12.8−1.7=1.1 and 3.9−2.8=1.13.9 - 2.8 = 1.13.9−2.8=1.1 ✔.

  4. Answer a=0.6a = 0.6a=0.6, d=1.1d = 1.1d=1.1

    Common trap: Lining up the decimal points wrongly when subtracting. Write 1.7−0.61.7 - 0.61.7−0.6 with the points under each other: 1.11.11.1.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (i)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(i) 2,4,8,16,…2, 4, 8, 16, \ldots2,4,8,16,…

Given: a list. Asked: AP or not; if AP, d and three more terms.

Concept used: every difference must be equal (Topic 2). Why it applies: this is the test for an AP.

  1. 1

    Differences: 4−2=24 - 2 = 24−2=2, 8−4=48 - 4 = 48−4=4, 16−8=816 - 8 = 816−8=8. Not equal.

  2. Check: each term is twice the one before — a multiplying pattern ✔.

  3. Answer Not an AP.

    Common trap: Seeing "2,42, 42,4" (difference 2) and continuing 6,8,…6, 8, \ldots6,8,… without checking the next pair.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (ii)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(ii) 2,52,3,72,…2, \dfrac{5}{2}, 3, \dfrac{7}{2}, \ldots2,25​,3,27​,…

Given: a list. Asked: AP or not; d and three more terms.

Concept used: check every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: the list mixes whole numbers and halves.

  1. 1

    Write every term in halves: 42,52,62,72\dfrac{4}{2}, \dfrac{5}{2}, \dfrac{6}{2}, \dfrac{7}{2}24​,25​,26​,27​.

  2. 2

    Each difference is 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​, so it is an AP with d=12d = \dfrac{1}{2}d=21​.

  3. 3

    Next three terms: 82=4\dfrac{8}{2} = 428​=4, 92\dfrac{9}{2}29​, 102=5\dfrac{10}{2} = 5210​=5.

  4. Check: 5−2=3=6×125 - 2 = 3 = 6 \times \dfrac{1}{2}5−2=3=6×21​, six steps from the 1st term to the 7th ✔.

  5. Answer AP, d=12d = \dfrac{1}{2}d=21​; next terms 4,92,54, \dfrac{9}{2}, 54,29​,5

    Common trap: Thinking the pattern "whole number, fraction, whole number" cannot be an AP. Write all terms with one denominator first.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (iii)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(iii) −1.2,−3.2,−5.2,−7.2,…-1.2, -3.2, -5.2, -7.2, \ldots−1.2,−3.2,−5.2,−7.2,…

Given: a list. Asked: AP or not; d and three more terms.

Concept used: check every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: this is the AP test.

  1. 1

    Differences: −3.2−(−1.2)=−2-3.2 - (-1.2) = -2−3.2−(−1.2)=−2, −5.2−(−3.2)=−2-5.2 - (-3.2) = -2−5.2−(−3.2)=−2, −7.2−(−5.2)=−2-7.2 - (-5.2) = -2−7.2−(−5.2)=−2. All equal: AP with d=−2d = -2d=−2.

  2. 2

    Next three terms: −9.2,−11.2,−13.2-9.2, -11.2, -13.2−9.2,−11.2,−13.2.

  3. Check: −13.2=−1.2+6×(−2)-13.2 = -1.2 + 6 \times (-2)−13.2=−1.2+6×(−2) ✔.

  4. Answer AP, d=−2d = -2d=−2; next terms −9.2,−11.2,−13.2-9.2, -11.2, -13.2−9.2,−11.2,−13.2

    Common trap: Writing d=2d = 2d=2 because "the numbers go up by 2". Their sizes grow, but the numbers go down.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (iv)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(iv) −10,−6,−2,2,…-10, -6, -2, 2, \ldots−10,−6,−2,2,…

Given: a list. Asked: AP or not; d and three more terms.

Concept used: check every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: this is the AP test.

  1. 1

    Differences: −6−(−10)=4-6 - (-10) = 4−6−(−10)=4, −2−(−6)=4-2 - (-6) = 4−2−(−6)=4, 2−(−2)=42 - (-2) = 42−(−2)=4. AP with d=4d = 4d=4.

  2. 2

    Next three terms: 6,10,146, 10, 146,10,14.

  3. Check: 14=−10+6×414 = -10 + 6 \times 414=−10+6×4 ✔.

  4. Answer AP, d=4d = 4d=4; next terms 6,10,146, 10, 146,10,14

    Common trap: −6−(−10)-6 - (-10)−6−(−10) worked out as −16-16−16. Subtracting −10-10−10 adds 10.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (v)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(v) 3,3+2,3+22,3+32,…3, 3 + \sqrt{2}, 3 + 2\sqrt{2}, 3 + 3\sqrt{2}, \ldots3,3+2​,3+22​,3+32​,…

Given: a list with surds. Asked: AP or not; d and three more terms.

Concept used: check every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: the 3's cancel when we subtract.

  1. 1

    Differences: (3+2)−3=2(3 + \sqrt{2}) - 3 = \sqrt{2}(3+2​)−3=2​, (3+22)−(3+2)=2(3 + 2\sqrt{2}) - (3 + \sqrt{2}) = \sqrt{2}(3+22​)−(3+2​)=2​, (3+32)−(3+22)=2(3 + 3\sqrt{2}) - (3 + 2\sqrt{2}) = \sqrt{2}(3+32​)−(3+22​)=2​. AP with d=2d = \sqrt{2}d=2​.

  2. 2

    Next three terms: 3+423 + 4\sqrt{2}3+42​, 3+523 + 5\sqrt{2}3+52​, 3+623 + 6\sqrt{2}3+62​.

  3. Check: the nth term is 3+(n−1)23 + (n - 1)\sqrt{2}3+(n−1)2​; for n=7n = 7n=7 it is 3+623 + 6\sqrt{2}3+62​ ✔.

  4. Answer AP, d=2d = \sqrt{2}d=2​; next terms 3+42,3+52,3+623 + 4\sqrt{2}, 3 + 5\sqrt{2}, 3 + 6\sqrt{2}3+42​,3+52​,3+62​

    Common trap: Adding 2\sqrt{2}2​ to the 3 as well, e.g. writing 32+423\sqrt{2} + 4\sqrt{2}32​+42​. Only the surd part grows.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (vi)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(vi) 0.2,0.22,0.222,0.2222,…0.2, 0.22, 0.222, 0.2222, \ldots0.2,0.22,0.222,0.2222,…

Given: a list of decimals. Asked: AP or not.

Concept used: check every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: this is the AP test.

  1. 1

    Differences: 0.22−0.2=0.020.22 - 0.2 = 0.020.22−0.2=0.02, 0.222−0.22=0.0020.222 - 0.22 = 0.0020.222−0.22=0.002, 0.2222−0.222=0.00020.2222 - 0.222 = 0.00020.2222−0.222=0.0002. Not equal.

  2. Check: each new digit adds a tenth of the previous addition — the steps shrink ✔.

  3. Answer Not an AP.

    Common trap: Thinking "add a 2 each time" is adding the same number. Adding a digit at the end adds a smaller amount every time.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (vii)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(vii) 0,−4,−8,−12,…0, -4, -8, -12, \ldots0,−4,−8,−12,…

Given: a list. Asked: AP or not; d and three more terms.

Concept used: check every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: this is the AP test.

  1. 1

    Differences: −4−0=−4-4 - 0 = -4−4−0=−4, −8−(−4)=−4-8 - (-4) = -4−8−(−4)=−4, −12−(−8)=−4-12 - (-8) = -4−12−(−8)=−4. AP with d=−4d = -4d=−4.

  2. 2

    Next three terms: −16,−20,−24-16, -20, -24−16,−20,−24.

  3. Check: −24=0+6×(−4)-24 = 0 + 6 \times (-4)−24=0+6×(−4) ✔.

  4. Answer AP, d=−4d = -4d=−4; next terms −16,−20,−24-16, -20, -24−16,−20,−24

    Common trap: Thinking an AP cannot start at 0. The first term can be any number.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (viii)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(viii) −12,−12,−12,−12,…-\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}, \ldots−21​,−21​,−21​,−21​,…

Given: a constant list. Asked: AP or not; d and three more terms.

Concept used: check every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: all differences are 0.

  1. 1

    Every difference is −12−(−12)=0-\dfrac{1}{2} - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0−21​−(−21​)=0. AP with d=0d = 0d=0.

  2. 2

    Next three terms: −12,−12,−12-\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}−21​,−21​,−21​.

  3. Check: adding 0 never changes the term ✔.

  4. Answer AP, d=0d = 0d=0; next terms −12,−12,−12-\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}−21​,−21​,−21​

    Common trap: Answering "not an AP because nothing changes". d=0d = 0d=0 is allowed.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (ix)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(ix) 1,3,9,27,…1, 3, 9, 27, \ldots1,3,9,27,…

Given: a list. Asked: AP or not.

Concept used: check every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: this is the AP test.

  1. 1

    Differences: 3−1=23 - 1 = 23−1=2, 9−3=69 - 3 = 69−3=6, 27−9=1827 - 9 = 1827−9=18. Not equal.

  2. Check: each term is 3 times the one before — a multiplying pattern ✔.

  3. Answer Not an AP.

    Common trap: Using only the first difference (2) and continuing 5,7,…5, 7, \ldots5,7,…
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (x)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(x) a,2a,3a,4a,…a, 2a, 3a, 4a, \ldotsa,2a,3a,4a,…

Given: a list in terms of a. Asked: AP or not; d and three more terms.

Concept used: simplify every difference (Topic 2). Why it applies: the terms are algebraic.

  1. 1

    Differences: 2a−a=a2a - a = a2a−a=a, 3a−2a=a3a - 2a = a3a−2a=a, 4a−3a=a4a - 3a = a4a−3a=a. AP with d=ad = ad=a (for every value of a).

  2. 2

    Next three terms: 5a,6a,7a5a, 6a, 7a5a,6a,7a.

  3. Check: the nth term is a+(n−1)a=naa + (n - 1)a = naa+(n−1)a=na; the 7th is 7a7a7a ✔.

  4. Answer AP, d=ad = ad=a; next terms 5a,6a,7a5a, 6a, 7a5a,6a,7a

    Common trap: Writing d=2ad = 2ad=2a (the second term) instead of the difference 2a−a2a - a2a−a.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (xi)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(xi) a,a2,a3,a4,…a, a^2, a^3, a^4, \ldotsa,a2,a3,a4,…

Given: a list of powers of a. Asked: AP or not.

Concept used: the first two differences must be equal (Topic 2). Why it applies: we can test when they are.

  1. 1

    Differences: a2−aa^2 - aa2−a and a3−a2a^3 - a^2a3−a2.

  2. 2

    These are equal only if a3−2a2+a=0a^3 - 2a^2 + a = 0a3−2a2+a=0, that is a(a−1)2=0a(a - 1)^2 = 0a(a−1)2=0: only when a=0a = 0a=0 or a=1a = 1a=1.

  3. 3

    For any other value of a (for example a=2a = 2a=2: 2,4,8,162, 4, 8, 162,4,8,16) the differences are not equal.

  4. Check: a=3a = 3a=3 gives 3,9,27,813, 9, 27, 813,9,27,81, with differences 6,18,546, 18, 546,18,54 — not equal ✔.

  5. Answer Not an AP in general. (Only in the special cases a=0a = 0a=0 or a=1a = 1a=1 does every term become the same, giving an AP with d=0d = 0d=0.)

    Common trap: Concluding "AP with d=ad = ad=a" from the look of the list. Powers multiply; they do not add a fixed amount.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (xii)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(xii) 2,8,18,32,…\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{8}, \sqrt{18}, \sqrt{32}, \ldots2​,8​,18​,32​,…

Given: a list of surds. Asked: AP or not; d and three more terms.

Concept used: simplify each surd, then check the differences (Topic 2). Why it applies: each is a whole number times 2\sqrt{2}2​.

  1. 1

    8=22\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}8​=22​, 18=32\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}18​=32​, 32=42\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}32​=42​. The list is 2,22,32,42\sqrt{2}, 2\sqrt{2}, 3\sqrt{2}, 4\sqrt{2}2​,22​,32​,42​.

  2. 2

    Each difference is 2\sqrt{2}2​: an AP with d=2d = \sqrt{2}d=2​.

  3. 3

    Next three terms: 52=505\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{50}52​=50​, 62=726\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{72}62​=72​, 72=987\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{98}72​=98​.

  4. Check: 50=25×2=52\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25 \times 2} = 5\sqrt{2}50​=25×2​=52​ ✔.

  5. Answer AP, d=2d = \sqrt{2}d=2​; next terms 50,72,98\sqrt{50}, \sqrt{72}, \sqrt{98}50​,72​,98​

    Common trap: Subtracting under the root: 8−2=6\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{6}8​−2​=6​. Simplify each surd first.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (xiii)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(xiii) 3,6,9,12,…\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{6}, \sqrt{9}, \sqrt{12}, \ldots3​,6​,9​,12​,…

Given: a list of surds. Asked: AP or not.

Concept used: check the differences (Topic 2). Why it applies: this is the AP test; here the surds do not simplify to multiples of one surd.

  1. 1

    6−3≈2.449−1.732=0.717\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{3} \approx 2.449 - 1.732 = 0.7176​−3​≈2.449−1.732=0.717.

  2. 2

    9−6=3−6≈3−2.449=0.551\sqrt{9} - \sqrt{6} = 3 - \sqrt{6} \approx 3 - 2.449 = 0.5519​−6​=3−6​≈3−2.449=0.551.

  3. 3

    The two differences are not equal, so it is not an AP.

  4. Check: the numbers under the roots go up by 3 each time (3,6,9,123, 6, 9, 123,6,9,12), but the roots themselves do not ✔.

  5. Answer Not an AP.

    Common trap: Thinking "3,6,9,123, 6, 9, 123,6,9,12 is an AP, so the square roots are too". Taking the square root breaks the equal steps.
Exercise 5.1, Q4 (xiv)1 mark

Which of the following are APs? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.

    The list is 1,9,25,491, 9, 25, 491,9,25,49.

  2. 2

    Differences: 8,16,248, 16, 248,16,24. Not equal.

    Substitute.

Exercise 5.2, Q42 marks

    Put an=0a_n = 0an​=0.

    0=8+(n−1)(−2)0 = 8 + (n - 1)(-2)0=8+(n−1)(−2)Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Subtract 8.

Exercise 5.2, Q102 marks

The 17th term of an AP exceeds its 10th term by 7. Find the common difference.

Given: a17−a10=7a_{17} - a_{10} = 7a17​−a10​=7. Asked: d.

Concept used: aq−ap=(q−p)da_q - a_p = (q - p)daq​−ap​=(q−p)d (Topic 3). Why it applies: "exceeds by 7" is a difference of two terms.

  1. 1

    Write both terms: a17=a+16da_{17} = a + 16da17​=a+16d, a10=a+9da_{10} = a + 9da10​=a+9d.

  2. 2

    Subtract: the a's cancel.

    (a+16d)−(a+9d)=7(a + 16d) - (a + 9d) = 7(a+16d)−(a+9d)=7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Simplify.

    7d=77d = 77d=7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Divide by 7.

    d=1d = 1d=1Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: with d=1d = 1d=1, the 17th term is 7 more than the 10th (7 steps of 1) ✔.

  6. Answer d=1d = 1d=1

    Common trap: Trying to find a first. It is not needed — and cannot be found: any AP with d=1d = 1d=1 works.

Exercise 5.2, Q122 marks

Two APs have the same common difference. The difference between their 100th terms is 100, what is the difference between their 1000th terms?

Given: first terms a and b, the same common difference d; a100−b100=100a_{100} - b_{100} = 100a100​−b100​=100. Asked: a1000−b1000a_{1000} - b_{1000}a1000​−b1000​.

Concept used: an=a+(n−1)da_n = a + (n - 1)dan​=a+(n−1)d (Topic 3). Why it applies: the d-parts cancel when the two nth terms are subtracted.

  1. 1

    a100−b100=(a+99d)−(b+99d)=a−ba_{100} - b_{100} = (a + 99d) - (b + 99d) = a - ba100​−b100​=(a+99d)−(b+99d)=a−b.

  2. 2

    So a−b=100a - b = 100a−b=100.

  3. 3

    a1000−b1000=(a+999d)−(b+999d)=a−b=100a_{1000} - b_{1000} = (a + 999d) - (b + 999d) = a - b = 100a1000​−b1000​=(a+999d)−(b+999d)=a−b=100.

  4. Check: take first terms 105 and 5 and d=2d = 2d=2: the 100th terms are 105+198=303105 + 198 = 303105+198=303 and 5+198=2035 + 198 = 2035+198=203 (difference 100); the 1000th terms are 105+1998=2103105 + 1998 = 2103105+1998=2103 and 5+1998=20035 + 1998 = 20035+1998=2003 (difference 100) ✔.

  5. Answer 100 — the difference between any two corresponding terms is the same.

    Common trap: Multiplying by 10 ("1000 is ten times 100, so 1000"). Equal steps keep the gap fixed.
Exercise 5.2, Q132 marks

Concept used: the multiples of 7 form an AP with d=7d = 7d=7; find n from the first and last (Topic 3). Why it applies: counting by listing would take too long.

    First: 7×15=1057 \times 15 = 1057×15=105. Last: 7×142=9947 \times 142 = 9947×142=994 (since 7×143=10017 \times 143 = 10017×143=1001).

    Put l=994l = 994l=994.

  3. 3

    Subtract 105.

  4. 4

    Divide by 7.

    127=n−1127 = n - 1127=n−1Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Add 1.

    n=128n = 128n=128Swipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: the multiples are 7×157 \times 157×15 to 7×1427 \times 1427×142: 142−15+1=128142 - 15 + 1 = 128142−15+1=128 numbers ✔.

    First multiple above 10: 12. Last below 250: 248.

    Put l=248l = 248l=248.

    Subtract (n−1)×2(n - 1) \times 2(n−1)×2 from both sides.

    Divide by 5.

    Add 1.

  4. 4

Concept used: a list is an AP if an+1−ana_{n+1} - a_nan+1​−an​ is the same for every n (Topic 2); then Sn=n2(a+l)S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)Sn​=2n​(a+l) (Topic 4). Why it applies: the nth term is given as a formula.

  1. 1

    an+1−an=[3+4(n+1)]−[3+4n]=4a_{n+1} - a_n = [3 + 4(n + 1)] - [3 + 4n] = 4an+1​−an​=[3+4(n+1)]−[3+4n]=4, the same for every n. So it is an AP with d=4d = 4d=4.

  2. 2

    a1=3+4=7a_1 = 3 + 4 = 7a1​=3+4=7 and a15=3+60=63a_{15} = 3 + 60 = 63a15​=3+60=63.

  3. 3

    S15=152(7+63)=152×70=525S_{15} = \dfrac{15}{2}(7 + 63) = \dfrac{15}{2} \times 70 = 525S15​=215​(7+63)=215​×70=525.

  4. Check: the list 7,11,15,…7, 11, 15, \ldots7,11,15,… has a+14d=7+56=63a + 14d = 7 + 56 = 63a+14d=7+56=63 ✔.

  5. Answer AP with d=4d = 4d=4; S15=525S_{15} = 525S15​=525

    Common trap: Taking the first term as 3 (the constant in the formula). The first term is a1=3+4×1=7a_1 = 3 + 4 \times 1 = 7a1​=3+4×1=7.
Exercise 5.3, Q10 (ii)3 marks

Show that a1,a2,…,an,…a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n, \ldotsa1​,a2​,…,an​,… form an AP where ana_nan​ is defined as below :

Also find the sum of the first 15 terms in each case.

Concept used: an+1−ana_{n+1} - a_nan+1​−an​ constant ⇒ AP (Topic 2); then SnS_nSn​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: the nth term is given as a formula.

    an+1−an=[9−5(n+1)]−[9−5n]=−5a_{n+1} - a_n = [9 - 5(n + 1)] - [9 - 5n] = -5an+1​−an​=[9−5(n+1)]−[9−5n]=−5, the same for every n. So it is an AP with d=−5d = -5d=−5.

    S15=152(4−66)=152×(−62)=−465S_{15} = \dfrac{15}{2}(4 - 66) = \dfrac{15}{2} \times (-62) = -465S15​=215​(4−66)=215​×(−62)=−465.

Exercise 5.3, Q113 marks

If the sum of the first n terms of an AP is 4n−n24n - n^24n−n2, what is the first term (that is S1S_1S1​)? What is the sum of first two terms? What is the second term? Similarly, find the 3rd, the 10th and the nth terms.

Given: Sn=4n−n2S_n = 4n - n^2Sn​=4n−n2. Asked: S1S_1S1​, S2S_2S2​, a2a_2a2​, a3a_3a3​, a10a_{10}a10​, ana_nan​.

Concept used: a1=S1a_1 = S_1a1​=S1​ and an=Sn−Sn−1a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}an​=Sn​−Sn−1​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: each term is the difference of two neighbouring sums.

    S1=4−1=3S_1 = 4 - 1 = 3S1​=4−1=3, so a1=3a_1 = 3a1​=3.

    S2=8−4=4S_2 = 8 - 4 = 4S2​=8−4=4, so a2=S2−S1=4−3=1a_2 = S_2 - S_1 = 4 - 3 = 1a2​=S2​−S1​=4−3=1.

  3. 3

    S3=12−9=3S_3 = 12 - 9 = 3S3​=12−9=3, so a3=S3−S2=3−4=−1a_3 = S_3 - S_2 = 3 - 4 = -1a3​=S3​−S2​=3−4=−1.

    S10=40−100=−60S_{10} = 40 - 100 = -60S10​=40−100=−60 and S9=36−81=−45S_9 = 36 - 81 = -45S9​=36−81=−45, so a10=−60−(−45)=−15a_{10} = -60 - (-45) = -15a10​=−60−(−45)=−15.

    In general:

    Expand the second bracket: 4n−4−(n2−2n+1)=−n2+6n−54n - 4 - (n^2 - 2n + 1) = -n^2 + 6n - 54n−4−(n2−2n+1)=−n2+6n−5.

    an=4n−n2+n2−6n+5a_n = 4n - n^2 + n^2 - 6n + 5an​=4n−n2+n2−6n+5Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Answer S1=a1=3S_1 = a_1 = 3S1​=a1​=3; S2=4S_2 = 4S2​=4; a2=1a_2 = 1a2​=1; a3=−1a_3 = -1a3​=−1; a10=−15a_{10} = -15a10​=−15; an=5−2na_n = 5 - 2nan​=5−2n

Exercise 5.3, Q122 marks

Find the sum of the first 40 positive integers divisible by 6.

Given: 6,12,18,…6, 12, 18, \ldots6,12,18,…; 40 terms. Asked: the sum.

Concept used: multiples of 6 form an AP with a=6a = 6a=6, d=6d = 6d=6 (Topic 4). Why it applies: we add the first 40 terms.

    The last term: a40=6×40=240a_{40} = 6 \times 40 = 240a40​=6×40=240.

    S40=402(6+240)=20×246=4920S_{40} = \dfrac{40}{2}(6 + 240) = 20 \times 246 = 4920S40​=240​(6+240)=20×246=4920.

Exercise 5.3, Q153 marks

A contract on construction job specifies a penalty for delay of completion beyond a certain date as follows: ₹ 200 for the first day, ₹ 250 for the second day, ₹ 300 for the third day, etc., the penalty for each succeeding day being ₹ 50 more than for the preceding day. Exercise 5.3, Q173 marks

In a school, students thought of planting trees in and around the school to reduce air pollution. It was decided that the number of trees, that each section of each class will plant, will be the same as the class, in which they are studying, e.g., a section of Class I will plant 1 tree, a section of Class II will plant 2 trees and so on till Class XII. Given: a section of Class k plants k trees; 3 sections per class; Classes I to XII. Asked: the total number of trees.

Concept used: trees per class form an AP: 3,6,9,…,363, 6, 9, \ldots, 363,6,9,…,36; the total is S12S_{12}S12​ (Topic 5). Why it applies: each class plants 3 more trees than the class below.

    Class I plants 3×1=33 \times 1 = 33×1=3 trees, Class II 3×2=63 \times 2 = 63×2=6, …, Class XII 3×12=363 \times 12 = 363×12=36.

  2. 2

    S12=122(3+36)=6×39=234S_{12} = \dfrac{12}{2}(3 + 36) = 6 \times 39 = 234S12​=212​(3+36)=6×39=234.

  3. Check: 3×(1+2+⋯+12)=3×78=2343 \times (1 + 2 + \cdots + 12) = 3 \times 78 = 2343×(1+2+⋯+12)=3×78=234 ✔.

  4. Answer 234 trees

    Common trap: Forgetting the three sections and answering 78.

A spiral is made up of successive semicircles, with centres alternately at A and B, starting with centre at A, of radii 0.5 cm, 1.0 cm, 1.5 cm, 2.0 cm, . . . as shown in Fig. 5.4. Concept used: the length of a semicircle of radius r is πr\pi rπr; the lengths form an AP; the total is S13S_{13}S13​ (Topic 5). Why it applies: the radii go up by 0.5 cm each time, so the lengths go up by 0.5π0.5\pi0.5π.

    Lengths: π×0.5, π×1.0, π×1.5,…\pi \times 0.5, \ \pi \times 1.0, \ \pi \times 1.5, \ldotsπ×0.5, π×1.0, π×1.5,… — an AP with a=0.5πa = 0.5\pia=0.5π, d=0.5πd = 0.5\pid=0.5π, n=13n = 13n=13.

  2. 2

    Total =π×(0.5+1.0+⋯+6.5)= \pi \times (0.5 + 1.0 + \cdots + 6.5)=π×(0.5+1.0+⋯+6.5).

  3. 3

    The sum of the radii: 132(0.5+6.5)=132×7=45.5\dfrac{13}{2}(0.5 + 6.5) = \dfrac{13}{2} \times 7 = 45.5213​(0.5+6.5)=213​×7=45.5.

  4. 4

    Total length =227×45.5=22×6.5=143= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 45.5 = 22 \times 6.5 = 143=722​×45.5=22×6.5=143 cm.

  5. Check: the 13th radius is 0.5+12×0.5=6.50.5 + 12 \times 0.5 = 6.50.5+12×0.5=6.5 cm ✔.

Exercise 5.3, Q19The pile of logs3 marks

200 logs are stacked in the following manner: 20 logs in the bottom row, 19 in the next row, 18 in the row next to it and so on (see Fig. 5.5). In how many rows are the 200 logs placed and how many logs are in the top row?

    Substitute.

    Expand.

Exercise 5.3, Q20The potato race3 marks

In a potato race, a bucket is placed at the starting point, which is 5 m from the first potato, and the other potatoes are placed 3 m apart in a straight line. There are ten potatoes in the line (see Fig. 5.6).
A competitor starts from the bucket, picks up the nearest potato, runs back with it, drops it in the bucket, runs back to pick up the next potato, runs to the bucket to drop it in, and she continues in the same way until all the potatoes are in the bucket. What is the total distance the competitor has to run?
[Hint : To pick up the first potato and the second potato, the total distance (in metres) run by a competitor is 2×5+2×(5+3)2 \times 5 + 2 \times (5 + 3)2×5+2×(5+3)]

Given: potatoes at 5 m, 8 m, 11 m, … from the bucket; 10 potatoes. Asked: total distance.

Concept used: one term = the round trip for one potato; the total is S10S_{10}S10​ (Topic 5). Why it applies: each potato is 3 m further, so each round trip is 6 m longer.

  1. 1

    Round trips (in m): 2×5=102 \times 5 = 102×5=10, 2×8=162 \times 8 = 162×8=16, 2×11=222 \times 11 = 222×11=22, … So a=10a = 10a=10, d=6d = 6d=6, n=10n = 10n=10.

  2. 2

    Substitute.

    S10=102[20+9×6]S_{10} = \dfrac{10}{2}[20 + 9 \times 6]S10​=210​[20+9×6]Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Work it out.

    S10=5×74=370S_{10} = 5 \times 74 = 370S10​=5×74=370Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: the last potato is 5+9×3=325 + 9 \times 3 = 325+9×3=32 m away, so the last trip is 64 m; 102(10+64)=370\dfrac{10}{2}(10 + 64) = 370210​(10+64)=370 ✔.

  5. Answer 370 m

    Common trap: Counting each potato one way only (185 m). She runs there and back every time.

Challenge — not for the exam: Exercise 5.4 (Optional)

Beyond the exam

NCERT marks Exercise 5.4 as optional, with the note "These exercises are not from the examination point of view." These five questions use only the ideas of this chapter, but they need more steps and more care. Try them for the challenge; they are not part of the board exam, and none of the practice, test or revision questions depend on them.

Exercise 5.4, Q1The first negative term (challenge)3 marks

Which term of the AP : 121,117,113,…121, 117, 113, \ldots121,117,113,…, is its first negative term?
[Hint : Find n for an<0a_n < 0an​<0]

Given: a=121a = 121a=121, d=−4d = -4d=−4. Asked: the position of the first term that is less than 0.

Concept used: solve the inequality an<0a_n < 0an​<0 and take the smallest whole number n that satisfies it (Topic 3). Why it applies: the terms fall by 4 each time, so once they go below 0 they stay below.

    Write ana_nan​.

    an=121+(n−1)(−4)=125−4na_n = 121 + (n - 1)(-4) = 125 - 4nan​=121+(n−1)(−4)=125−4nSwipe to see the whole equation →

    We need an<0a_n < 0an​<0.

    125−4n<0125 - 4n < 0125−4n<0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Add 4n4n4n to both sides.

    125<4n125 < 4n125<4nSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Divide by 4 (a positive number, so the sign <<< stays).

    n>3114n > 31\dfrac{1}{4}n>3141​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    The smallest whole number greater than 311431\dfrac{1}{4}3141​ is 32.

  6. Check: a31=125−124=1a_{31} = 125 - 124 = 1a31​=125−124=1 (still positive) and a32=125−128=−3a_{32} = 125 - 128 = -3a32​=125−128=−3 (negative) ✔.

Exercise 5.4, Q2A sum and a product (challenge)4 marks

The sum of the third and the seventh terms of an AP is 6 and their product is 8. Find the sum of first sixteen terms of the AP.

Given: a3+a7=6a_3 + a_7 = 6a3​+a7​=6, a3×a7=8a_3 \times a_7 = 8a3​×a7​=8. Asked: S16S_{16}S16​.

Concept used: write a3=a+2da_3 = a + 2da3​=a+2d and a7=a+6da_7 = a + 6da7​=a+6d; the sum gives a+4da + 4da+4d; the product then gives d (Topics 3–4). Why it applies: two facts, two unknowns — one of the equations is quadratic.

  1. 1

    Sum: (a+2d)+(a+6d)=6(a + 2d) + (a + 6d) = 6(a+2d)+(a+6d)=6, so 2a+8d=62a + 8d = 62a+8d=6.

    a+4d=3a + 4d = 3a+4d=3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Write a3a_3a3​ and a7a_7a7​ using a=3−4da = 3 - 4da=3−4d: a3=3−2da_3 = 3 - 2da3​=3−2d and a7=3+2da_7 = 3 + 2da7​=3+2d.

  3. 3

    Product.

    (3−2d)(3+2d)=8(3 - 2d)(3 + 2d) = 8(3−2d)(3+2d)=8Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Expand.

    9−4d2=89 - 4d^2 = 89−4d2=8Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Rearrange.

    d2=14d^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}d2=41​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    So d=12d = \dfrac{1}{2}d=21​ or d=−12d = -\dfrac{1}{2}d=−21​. Both give real APs, so find S16S_{16}S16​ for each.

  7. 7

    d=12d = \dfrac{1}{2}d=21​: a=3−2=1a = 3 - 2 = 1a=3−2=1; S16=162[2+15×12]=8×192=76S_{16} = \dfrac{16}{2}\left[2 + 15 \times \dfrac{1}{2}\right] = 8 \times \dfrac{19}{2} = 76S16​=216​[2+15×21​]=8×219​=76.

  8. 8

    d=−12d = -\dfrac{1}{2}d=−21​: a=3+2=5a = 3 + 2 = 5a=3+2=5; S16=162[10+15×(−12)]=8×52=20S_{16} = \dfrac{16}{2}\left[10 + 15 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right] = 8 \times \dfrac{5}{2} = 20S16​=216​[10+15×(−21​)]=8×25​=20.

  9. Check: first AP 1,1.5,2,…1, 1.5, 2, \ldots1,1.5,2,…: its 3rd and 7th terms are 2 and 4 (sum 6, product 8) ✔. Second AP 5,4.5,4,…5, 4.5, 4, \ldots5,4.5,4,…: its 3rd and 7th terms are 4 and 2 ✔.

  10. Answer S16=76S_{16} = 76S16​=76 (when d=12d = \dfrac{1}{2}d=21​) or S16=20S_{16} = 20S16​=20 (when d=−12d = -\dfrac{1}{2}d=−21​)

    Common trap: Taking only d=12d = \dfrac{1}{2}d=21​. The question does not say whether the AP increases or decreases, so both values of d are possible.
Exercise 5.4, Q3The ladder (challenge)3 marks

A ladder has rungs 25 cm apart. (see Fig. 5.7). The rungs decrease uniformly in length from 45 cm at the bottom to 25 cm at the top. If the top and the bottom rungs are 2122\dfrac{1}{2}221​ m apart, what is the length of the wood required for the rungs?
[Hint : Number of rungs =25025+1= \dfrac{250}{25} + 1=25250​+1]

Fig. 5.7 (described): a ladder narrowing towards the top; the bottom rung is marked 45 cm and the top rung 25 cm; the distance from the bottom rung to the top rung is marked 2122\dfrac{1}{2}221​ m, and the gap between two neighbouring rungs 25 cm.

Given: rungs 25 cm apart; bottom rung 45 cm, top rung 25 cm; 2122\dfrac{1}{2}221​ m = 250 cm from bottom rung to top rung. Asked: the total length of the rungs.

Concept used: the rung lengths form an AP from 45 to 25; count the rungs, then Sn=n2(a+l)S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)Sn​=2n​(a+l) (Topic 4). Why it applies: "decrease uniformly" means by the same amount each time.

  1. 1

    Number of gaps between the bottom and top rungs: 25025=10\dfrac{250}{25} = 1025250​=10.

  2. 2

    Number of rungs = gaps + 1 = 11.

  3. 3

    Total length.

    S11=112(45+25)=112×70=385S_{11} = \dfrac{11}{2}(45 + 25) = \dfrac{11}{2} \times 70 = 385S11​=211​(45+25)=211​×70=385Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: with 11 rungs, d=25−4510=−2d = \dfrac{25 - 45}{10} = -2d=1025−45​=−2 cm; the lengths 45,43,…,2545, 43, \ldots, 2545,43,…,25 add up to 385 ✔.

  5. Answer 385 cm of wood (3.85 m)

    Common trap: Taking 10 rungs (the number of gaps), which gives 102(45+25)=350\dfrac{10}{2}(45 + 25) = 350210​(45+25)=350 cm. Ten gaps need 11 rungs — one at each end.
Exercise 5.4, Q4The houses in a row (challenge)4 marks

The houses of a row are numbered consecutively from 1 to 49. Show that there is a value of x such that the sum of the numbers of the houses preceding the house numbered x is equal to the sum of the numbers of the houses following it. Find this value of x.
[Hint : Sx−1=S49−SxS_{x-1} = S_{49} - S_xSx−1​=S49​−Sx​]

Given: houses 1,2,…,491, 2, \ldots, 491,2,…,49. Asked: x with (sum of 111 to x−1x - 1x−1) = (sum of x+1x + 1x+1 to 49).

Concept used: 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)21 + 2 + \cdots + n = \dfrac{n(n + 1)}{2}1+2+⋯+n=2n(n+1)​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: both sides are sums of consecutive whole numbers.

  1. 1

    Houses before x: Sx−1=(x−1)x2S_{x-1} = \dfrac{(x - 1)x}{2}Sx−1​=2(x−1)x​.

  2. 2

    Houses after x: S49−Sx=49×502−x(x+1)2=1225−x(x+1)2S_{49} - S_x = \dfrac{49 \times 50}{2} - \dfrac{x(x + 1)}{2} = 1225 - \dfrac{x(x + 1)}{2}S49​−Sx​=249×50​−2x(x+1)​=1225−2x(x+1)​.

  3. 3

    Set them equal and multiply by 2.

    (x−1)x=2450−x(x+1)(x - 1)x = 2450 - x(x + 1)(x−1)x=2450−x(x+1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Expand both sides.

    x2−x=2450−x2−xx^2 - x = 2450 - x^2 - xx2−x=2450−x2−xSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Add x2+xx^2 + xx2+x to both sides.

    2x2=24502x^2 = 24502x2=2450Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Divide by 2.

    x2=1225x^2 = 1225x2=1225Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    x=35x = 35x=35 (a house number is positive, so reject −35-35−35). Since 35 is a whole number between 1 and 49, such a house exists.

  8. Check: 1+2+⋯+34=34×352=5951 + 2 + \cdots + 34 = \dfrac{34 \times 35}{2} = 5951+2+⋯+34=234×35​=595 and 36+37+⋯+49=1225−630=59536 + 37 + \cdots + 49 = 1225 - 630 = 59536+37+⋯+49=1225−630=595 ✔.

  9. Answer x=35x = 35x=35

    Common trap: Including house x itself on one side. The hint's S49−SxS_{49} - S_xS49​−Sx​ leaves house x out of both sums.
Exercise 5.4, Q5The terrace (challenge)4 marks

A small terrace at a football ground comprises of 15 steps each of which is 50 m long and built of solid concrete.
Each step has a rise of 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ m and a tread of 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ m. (see Fig. 5.8). Calculate the total volume of concrete required to build the terrace.
[Hint : Volume of concrete required to build the first step =14×12×50= \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 50=41​×21​×50 m³]

Fig. 5.8 (described): a flight of 15 solid steps seen from the side, each 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ m higher than the one in front of it and 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ m deep, and 50 m long.

Given: 15 steps; each is 50 m long, 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ m deep (tread); the kth step stands k4\dfrac{k}{4}4k​ m high from the ground. Asked: the total volume.

Concept used: each step is a solid cuboid; the volumes form an AP; the total is S15S_{15}S15​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: each step is 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ m taller than the one before, with the same depth and length.

  1. 1

    Volume of the kth step =k4×12×50=25k4= \dfrac{k}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 50 = \dfrac{25k}{4}=4k​×21​×50=425k​ m³.

  2. 2

    The volumes are 254,504,754,…\dfrac{25}{4}, \dfrac{50}{4}, \dfrac{75}{4}, \ldots425​,450​,475​,… — an AP with a=254a = \dfrac{25}{4}a=425​, d=254d = \dfrac{25}{4}d=425​, n=15n = 15n=15.

  3. 3

    The last volume: 25×154=3754\dfrac{25 \times 15}{4} = \dfrac{375}{4}425×15​=4375​.

  4. 4

    Total.

    S15=152(254+3754)=152×100=750S_{15} = \dfrac{15}{2}\left(\dfrac{25}{4} + \dfrac{375}{4}\right) = \dfrac{15}{2} \times 100 = 750S15​=215​(425​+4375​)=215​×100=750Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: 254×(1+2+⋯+15)=254×120=750\dfrac{25}{4} \times (1 + 2 + \cdots + 15) = \dfrac{25}{4} \times 120 = 750425​×(1+2+⋯+15)=425​×120=750 ✔.

  6. Answer 750 m³ of concrete

    Common trap: Giving every step the same volume (15×254=93.7515 \times \dfrac{25}{4} = 93.7515×425​=93.75 m³). Each step is a block from the ground up, so higher steps are taller blocks.
